accident_report:
Vehicle Initialization
On a three-lane one-way urban expressway (lanes numbered 1 to 3 from right to left), the road has a 5% uphill grade. It is nighttime with no street lighting, and the roadway is wet due to ongoing rain, resulting in reduced tire-road friction.
V1 is traveling in lane 2 at 78 km/h, positioned mid-stream in traffic, intending to overtake slower vehicles ahead and maintain a higher cruising speed.
V2 follows V1 in lane 2 at a distance of approximately 18 meters, traveling at 80 km/h, maintaining a close following distance without adequate safety margin.
V3 is in lane 1, about 25 meters ahead of V1, moving at 55 km/h. Due to the uphill grade, its acceleration capability is limited, and it maintains a relatively low speed.
V4 is in lane 3, slightly behind V1 by about 10 meters, traveling steadily at 85 km/h with no immediate intention to change lanes.
Scenario Development
Because of the uphill grade, V3 travels significantly slower than V1, creating a large longitudinal speed difference. Under low nighttime visibility, V1 misjudges the speed and distance to V3 and only realizes the closing gap at a relatively short distance. To avoid slowing down, V1 checks left and notices V4 approaching in lane 3 but underestimates its speed and distance, deciding to change lanes to overtake.
On the wet surface, V1’s lane change is less stable and takes longer to complete. Meanwhile, V4, limited by nighttime visibility, detects V1 merging into its lane when the gap has already reduced to about 12 meters. V4 applies moderate braking, reducing speed from 85 km/h to 78 km/h.
After overtaking V3, V1 cannot accelerate effectively due to the uphill grade and fails to create sufficient distance from V4. V1 then attempts to return to lane 2 prematurely. Due to limited visibility and misjudgment of rear traffic, V1 cuts back into lane 2 with only about a 10-meter gap to V2.
V2, already following too closely at 80 km/h, has its forward view partially obstructed during V1’s cut-in. It detects V1’s deceleration only after the maneuver is completed. V2 initiates emergency braking, but the wet road significantly reduces available friction, limiting deceleration and only reducing speed to about 65 km/h.
At the same time, V1 slows further to about 60 km/h due to the presence of slower V3 ahead. This creates a rapid closing situation between V2 and V1 with insufficient stopping distance. V4, observing the deceleration chain in lane 2, attempts slight lateral adjustment but remains in lane 3 and continues braking.
Outcome
Ultimately, V2 fails to stop in time due to insufficient following distance, reduced braking efficiency on the wet surface, and the sudden gap reduction caused by V1’s unsafe cut-in. V2 rear-ends V1 at approximately 65 km/h while V1 is traveling at about 60 km/h. The collision occurs in lane 2, pushing V1 forward toward the slower V3 and creating a high risk of secondary collision. The crash results from the combined effects of uphill-induced speed differences, reduced nighttime visibility, diminished road friction, unsafe following behavior, and improper lane-changing maneuvers. Traffic in lane 2 becomes obstructed immediately, increasing the likelihood of secondary incidents behind.
